Posted May 7, 2002
(MarijuanaNews note: Below is an excerpt from an interview with John Walters from the Baltimore Sun. The questions are all soft-balls, of course, and as such this is just one more example of bad journalism. Recently I have posted similar statements by Walters.
See

However, I think that this adds another piece to the picture. He is saying that marijuana is a greater problem than methamphetamine!

Now, I have made very clear that I think that Walters is evil, to use George W. Bush's favorite word, which he uses to describe non-Administration employees who kill innocent Americans.

However, while one man's terrorist is another man's Drug Czar, Walters is a real world problem for the Bush Administration. They just don't know it yet. This man is such an ideologue that he is completely out of touch with the American people.

I often make the point that one of the major differences between us and the prohibitionists is that while they go out of their way to suppress or misrepresent the anti-prohibitionist position, we want and need for the public to know what the prohibitionists are saying, in their own words. That is why so much of MarijuanaNews is devoted to just that.

Walters is the chief strategist and propagandist for the war on freedom, but I have seen nothing that indicates that he has a clue about the current state of the public discourse on cannabis prohibition.

I want the American people to know that he thinks that marijuana is a worse problem than meth. Here it is, along with some of the other more bizarre lies that he has been pushing lately.)

Excerpted from The Baltimore Sun
May 4, 2002

By Del Quentin Wilber

Interview: The White House drug czar discusses his office's recent media campaign and its vision for the future.

The White House's Office of National Drug Control Policy, run by drug czar John P. Walters, has a media budget of $180 million to use in the war on drugs.

Reporter: Whom are you trying to reach to prevent drug use? And what drugs are at the root of this country's drug problem?

Walters: Of the 4.5 million who need to benefit from drug treatment in the United States, 23 percent are teen-agers. We've never had an estimate suggesting that high a percentage of people with substance abuse problems were that young.

Secondly, people have not talked about and focused on marijuana. Of the 65 percent of those people in that dependency category, their primary or secondary dependence is with marijuana.

(MarijuanaNews note: How this works. People in a " rehab " program are asked about their " drug of choice. "

To most people that means, which one do you like the most? When they say that cannabis is their favorite, to the rehab racketeers this means that it is " their primary or secondary dependence. " This justifies not only their " treatment " but also the arrest and " treatment " of others. If they deny that they are dependent then they are in denial and cannot get released from " treatment. " )

It is by far the single largest factor in illegal drug addiction in the country. ...

Reporter: How does that fit into the debate concerning medical use of marijuana?

Walters: The medical marijuana issue should be handled directly in the way that we do other things in medical science. We have the finest health care system in the world and in world history. We have very reliable ways of taking substances that have medical efficacy, proving that efficacy and safety. ... The medical marijuana debate has been used as an argument that officials are unjustly keeping people who are suffering from medicine. ... The problem is that the debate is sidetracking legitimate concerns about the drug, and people are suggesting that there is some kind of bigotry ... by those who express concerns about the drug.
(MarijuanaNews note: No follow up questions about the IOM report, or anything else.)
From 1999 see
The Party Line Versus Reality On Medical Marijuana.

Reporter: How seriously do you take methamphetamine as a problem, especially in rural America?

Walters: We take methamphetamine very seriously. ... From my view and my experience, when drug problems have spread and become very serious, it's because they have not been recognized having serious consequences early enough. It's safe; it's fun; it's not going to be a real threat. Methamphetamine has spread rapidly. It looks like it's coming from larger laboratories. Right now, it has not reached the level of cocaine or heroin or marijuana. But its seriousness is growing.
(MarijuanaNews note: The problem with this answer is that the politicians have been using meth to justify attacks on cannabis, because they know that the public knows the difference.)
